In Netflix’s Steps, out tomorrow, Cinderella’s stepsisters get to tell their side of the story. The change in perspective is familiar by now; we’ve seen it in other animated films, but directors Alyce Tzue and John Ripa make it their own with a few clever turns and a willingness to let both Cinderella and her stepsisters make mistakes. It’s a new version of the classic fairy tale where nobody is without their faults.

Lilith (Ali Wong) and Margot (Stephanie Hsu) are tired of living in Cinderella’s shadow, so Lilith steals the Fairy Godmother’s wand and upends the royal ball. That gives the ruthlessly poised Priscilla (Nikki Glaser) an opening to seize power, leaving Lilith forced to team up with Cinderella (Amanda Seyfried) to put things right.

Directed by Alyce Tzue and John Ripa, the CG feature is produced by Amy Poehler, Jane Hartwell, and Kim Lessing. The filmmakers looked to late-18th-century France for the kingdom of Alouette, building a Rococo world with the tactile detail of a miniature. Even the stucco had an unlikely reference in espresso foam.

Tzue and Ripa spoke with Cartoon Brew ahead of the film’s release about how its palette follows the power shift between Lilith and Cinderella, how a clockwork mech chase depends on what happens inside the machine, and what each director picked up from the other while working with a crew spread across time zones.

Cartoon Brew: Giving the stepsisters the lead could have been as simple as making them the heroes and Cinderella the villain. But we’ve seen that before. Instead, your stepsisters are complicated, three-dimensional characters, and you don’t let them off the hook for some of their more problematic behaviors. How did you work out where to take those characters?

Alyce Tzue: I do think you go in thinking that the stepsisters are just going to be misunderstood and good. But what we’re also trying to say is that while the stepsisters were rejected by the kingdom, they put up these emotional walls that end up being harmful to Cinderella. It’s a process of humanizing the fairy-tale archetypes, both for Lilith and Cinderella. Lilith isn’t good or evil. She’s just human. Similarly, Cinderella isn’t perfect. Neither is she evil. They’re all just very flawed.

John Ripa: Every character in our film is flawed in that way and has something to learn from the others. They have that opportunity to be themselves and be accepted for themselves, but they have to earn their way and earn the relationships.

The very distinct three acts of this film have equally singular looks, from the pinks and purples of the royal ball to the earthier palette once the characters leave the kingdom. How did you use color to follow the story?

Tzue: You start with the fairy tale that you might be more familiar with in Act One. In Act Two, you break the fairy tale. And then Act Three is, what is our version of it? When you reconstruct it, what is the modern message we want to get across? The color palettes definitely follow that pattern.

Ripa: It reflects the characters’ journey and their relationship as well. Lilith is trying to fit into Cinderella’s world in Act One, so there’s a lot that’s familiar. Then once the story breaks, Cinderella’s trying to fit into what Lilith is more comfortable with. At the end, it’s this meshing of everything. Everything in animation has to be planned. Our production designers and art directors and the layout and previs teams put a lot of thought into what all those things mean.

There is a lot of world building going on in this film. What gave your version of Cinderella its own look, from the surfaces in the kingdom to the shapes of the characters?

Tzue: Late-1700s France is the era of Marie Antoinette and “let them eat cake.” The Rococo era has always been aspirational for animation, I think. It’s very detailed and intricate. Jumping off of that, we wanted a 3D medium to look even more 3D. We miniaturized the textures and used references that weren’t literal. Espresso foam was the inspiration for our stucco, and sugar crystals were the inspiration for the colorful siding of a carriage. We used chocolate foil to make this world feel more decadent. Hopefully people will want to taste the movie with their eyes.

Ripa: Alyce was very intentional about pushing the shapes of the female characters. A lot of times you see that more with male characters. The shapes were very specific, and it allowed the female characters to have a range you don’t normally get.

Tzue: We had some fun guides for their head shapes. Lilith doesn’t have much of a chin. She’s a martini glass. Margot is kind of a lima bean. Her mom is a bit of a kite.

Priscilla is my favorite character in the film. She looks like the picture of a fairy-tale princess, despite her conflicting personality. How did that look feed into the way you wrote her?

Tzue: The design inspiration was definitely Paris Hilton meets Marie Antoinette. We wanted to create this kingdom of Alouette that had these sky-high standards for women in particular. You have to be poised and graceful and dance and walk with books on your head. Lilith rebels against that, but Priscilla is that on hyperdrive. She wants to be queen. She takes classes on every single thing. She thinks her face looks great on money. When you’re forced to fulfill these impossible expectations, that can turn you into a villain. It’s all you care about.

Ripa: We had incredible writers who really brought out her character and humor, and Nikki Glaser can deliver any line. She’s sarcastic and biting and witty. Priscilla is fun to watch and visually interesting. It was a collaboration with everybody.

Once the story leaves the ball, you bring in beasts, trolls, and a whole community outside the kingdom. What did that open up for you?

Ripa: Something really cool we learned on the film is that Cinderella’s story has this incredible history, and every version adds something. Charles Perrault’s version introduced the fairy godmother, the pumpkin, the glass slipper. It’s like that game of telephone where everybody adds something to the story. It’s almost like the longest story in development ever. We could give you something familiar and then break the story open to explore things the other versions hadn’t had the opportunity to.

Tzue: Margot turns into a frog. There are trolls that live under bridges and wolves that live in the forest. It’s iconography you associate with fairy tales, and yet it’s pretty chaotic because we broke the fairy tale and anything goes. Sometimes you have to break something apart and put it back together to see what you can modernize or make better. Traditional fairy tales elevate a certain sort of protagonist. By the end, it comes together as a love letter to fairy tales, and at the same time it’s saying, “Let’s include more people in the fairy tales.”

On that journey, the characters get around by goat and eventually by clockwork mech. How did you make machinery feel at home in a world built around magic?

Ripa: There was a lot of research into the time period and what they had. You look at some of the automatons that were built, especially in France, and the clockwork. We were really inspired by that. In Jeff’s world, you see a lot of those influences. We wanted you to feel like you were always in these characters’ world. It’s got some modern elements, but it’s also very French Rococo. We wanted to keep it grounded and believable.

Tzue: We wanted to contrast what it feels like to have magic and what it feels like to lose it. Magic is a symbol of privilege. Magic has helped Cinderella, and the moment she doesn’t have it, she has to walk on her bare feet. Now they have to have a goat. Now they have to have a mech. You can’t just have magic flying you across time and space. When you do have it, what do you choose to do with it? What’s your responsibility once you recognize what a privilege it is? That’s very much the message at the end.

The mech chase has a lot going on outside the machine, but there’s also an emotional scene happening inside it. How did you balance the two?

Tzue: That’s one of my favorite sequences. It was a lesson in prioritizing the character journey. Every time we paid too much attention to the action, you lost track of the emotions and didn’t get that catharsis at the end. That pattern kept repeating. We got feedback that Act One was too long, but when we took out setups, it just wasn’t as emotional. It was a long process of balancing those elements.

Ripa: Interesting characters make choices, and they have to deal with the consequences. Sometimes those choices are mistakes. Sometimes they hurt somebody. Then how do they resolve that? It can’t just be through words. They have to do things that help those relationships evolve. When you humanize the characters that way, you recognize a lot of your own relationships in them.

The palace and the forest feel like places you could set entire films in. How did you get that sense of scale with the resources you had?

Tzue: We had budget constraints, and we reused sets. We didn’t have much to work with in the palace, so we’d have to say, “Okay, we have to reuse this room.” We had a forest build, but we had to be smart about reusing parts of it and dressing them differently so you couldn’t tell. There were a lot of tricks you probably wouldn’t notice.

Ripa: We had digital matte painters who could fill out the background behind the trees with more trees or hills. We could add depth and layers and richness to the world that way. One of the challenges was finding that slight miniature feel in this incredibly ornate world. How do you get it in the textures, in the scale, when the characters are in a shot? That was a process of discovery.

Steps is the first film to come out of Netflix Animation’s end-to-end pipeline. What did that setup mean for you as directors working with teams across time zones?

Tzue: The challenges are what you might expect in terms of practicality. There are the time-zone differences and the transition from working with a vendor to bringing them in and fully unifying the teams. We feel very much like a community. What I’m most proud of visually are the textures, the decadence of the world, and the detail the artists put into bringing it to life.

Ripa: We definitely traveled a lot. You felt like you were living out of a suitcase sometimes. But to sit at somebody’s desk and point to the screen and talk to them, or sit in a room with the animators so they can see your expressions as you act something out, is some of the most rewarding stuff. It’s the best way to build trust, which you need when you’re dealing with different time zones and long distances.

What did you pick up from each other as directing partners?

Ripa: I’ve been doing this for over 30 years, and it was great to learn from Alyce’s strengths in working with actors, in editorial, and with music. She’s a great writer, too. She did a lot of the scratch for Ali Wong. You record scratch before you get the voices, and she was really able to lock into the character and the emotions and help create Lilith.

Tzue: I feel like a good partnership is when you have complementary skills and shared values. John taught me a lot about storytelling and what’s most important in a story. Landing the ending, working backward from there, always focusing on the emotional arcs. And then there’s his experience in animation, storyboarding, and cinematography. I do feel like it was a process of mutual osmosis. I feel very lucky to have been able to learn on the job with someone like John.

Disney has released its first trailer for Ice Age: Boiling Point, the sixth theatrical feature in the animated franchise born at Blue Sky Studios before the East Coast outfit was shuttered after the Fox acquisition. The film will hit theaters on February 5 of next year.

Those original films have endured in a way that few franchises ever manage to achieve, thanks to a heavy dose of humor, likable and memorable characters, and, for its time, sharp CG animation. The new film… well, we’ll let you decide how sharp you think the new film looks:

The story brings back Rudy, the dinosaur who terrorized Buck and the herd in 2009’s Ice Age: Dawn of the Dinosaurs (not Rudy, Sid’s cousin with an overbite). His species is now on the brink of extinction, and a pack of carnivores is targeting its eggs. The herd sets out to deliver one of those eggs to its nesting ground at the top of an active volcano in order to save the Lost World. For Manny and his friends, who are beginning to feel their age, it’s a return to the kind of adventure they used to have all the time.

It’s the franchise’s third visit to the Lost World, following Dawn of the Dinosaurs and the 2022 Disney+ spinoff The Ice Age Adventures of Buck Wild. John C. Donkin, who directed the spinoff, returns to direct, with longtime series producer Lori Forte producing.

Ray Romano, John Leguizamo, Denis Leary, and Queen Latifah reprise their roles as Manny, Sid, Diego, and Ellie, respectively. Simon Pegg returns as Buck, the one-eyed weasel who knows his way around the Lost World.

Welcome to Cartoon Brew’s series of spotlights focusing on the animated shorts that have qualified for the 2027 Oscars. The films in this series have qualified through one of multiple routes: by winning an Oscar-qualifying award at a film festival, by exhibiting theatrically, or by winning a Student Academy Award.

Today’s short is Danse Macabre, written and directed by Hisko Hulsing, whose credits include Undone and The Sandman episode “A Dream of a Thousand Cats.” Produced by Valk Productions with Autour de Minuit, Vivi Film, and Cinemon Entertainment, the film combines oil paintings, 2D animation, and CG, with machine-learning tools trained on Hulsing’s paintings used to polish its painterly textures. The film, one of the most consequential and controversial debuts at Annecy over the summer, qualified for the upcoming Oscars through a theatrical run.

Set to the second movement of Dmitri Shostakovich’s Tenth Symphony, the film follows an army of skeletons from an orderly march into catastrophic violence. Hulsing began developing it in response to Russia’s invasion of Crimea and what he saw as a resurgence of fascism. Orchestral music dictated its structure, while his study of 17th-century Dutch painting shaped a world intended to exist beyond the screen through exhibitions and orchestral performances.

Cartoon Brew: What was it about this story or concept that connected with you and compelled you to direct the film?

Hisko Hulsing: Twelve years ago, when Russia invaded Crimea and started a war in Ukraine, I began following what was happening in Russia. Putin’s expansionism, the suppression of his own people, and the murder of others seemed like a resurrection of fascism to me. To prepare people’s minds, demons from the past were unearthed; figures like Beria and Stalin were being rehabilitated. I saw this approach being copied by far-right groups in Europe and politicians in the U.S. I wanted to create a nightmarish film to warn people about these tendencies. Sadly, reality has surpassed my apocalyptic vision.

What did you learn through the experience of making this film, either production-wise, filmmaking-wise, creatively, or about the subject matter?

This was a very complex film to make. Eighty people from six studios worked on it in the Netherlands, France, Belgium, and Hungary. All animation was done with traditional software like Blender, Houdini, and TVPaint, and we developed new techniques to create painterly textures for the traditional animation using machine-learning tools trained on my own paintings.

Being one of the first artists to do so was met not with the praise I naively expected, but with protest. I’m curious how many of the protesters will use similar tools once they’ve been implemented in software like Blender.

Can you describe how you developed your visual approach to the film? Why did you settle on this style and technique?

As with all my films and series, my oil paintings form the basis for the look of the film.

I’ve studied 17th-century Dutch painters for decades and developed a very classical technique. I love the organic, warm nature of real paint, which allows me to create mysterious and dreamy worlds. For Danse Macabre, I painted all the characters into the paintings, which is unusual.

I made an oil painting for each shot and removed the characters after photographing them. Danse Macabre is a film, but it will also be a traveling exhibition and a series of orchestral performances.

How closely did Shostakovich’s music dictate the film’s editing, choreography, and pacing? And how did you adapt the instrumental piece into a cohesive narrative?

Shostakovich’s music dictated almost everything. I was constantly listening to this scherzo to come up with ideas and images. The film doesn’t follow a classical narrative, but there’s still a strong structure derived directly from the music. It starts with a march, an appearance of military order and intentionality, but soon descends into chaos, panic, and total destruction, as most wars do.

Some say this Allegro was meant to be a terrifying portrait of mass killer Joseph Stalin. I didn’t take that literally, but I tried to stay as truthful as possible to this beautiful and terrifying piece of music.

Netflix has released the first trailer for Living the Dream, its new adult animated workplace sitcom from Apple & Onion creator George Gendi and Hanna-Barbera Studios Europe.

Set to hit the platform on Friday, December 18, the show’s official synopsis reads:

Best friends Des and Ray are a couple of really cool guys from London who should have made it big by now but haven’t but still could. Instead they’re stuck at a we’re-gonna-save-the-planet type company called Ecofood, doing “social media” for hardly any money. Now they must navigate awkward workplace romance, HR blunders, directives from the L.A. office and Ray’s dad’s disapproval. Could be worse, but could be much, much better.

Gendi created, co-wrote, and executive produced the series. In a release, he explained:

Living the Dream has been a labor of love, and Netflix has been a great partner. I look forward to introducing audiences around the world to this lovable group of characters and to the joys of London office culture

He also voices one of its characters alongside Javone Prince, Julia Davis, Tom Stourton, Ellie White, Ambika Mod, Chris Diamantopoulos, and Stavros Halkias. Ireland’s Boulder Media (Captain Fall, Cat Burglar) handled animation. Sam Register, Sarah Fell, and Daniel Lennard also serve as executive producers.

Heeboo, a new digital platform launched by the team behind Claynosaurz, has unveiled its first slate of creator-owned properties. The Book of Life director Jorge R. Gutiérrez headlines the lineup with the adult animated project El Guapo vs. the Narco Vampires. Goldie creator Emily Brundige joins with Strawberry Vampire, and Agora Studio is bringing its creature comedy Zooya.

Announced in October, Heeboo is built as a site where animators can introduce their characters and stories, share works in progress, and build a following while their projects are still in development. Fans can enter creative challenges and earn rewards for taking part. The idea comes from Claynosaurz itself, which used sales of digital collectibles to fund more animation and gave fans a role in the shorts by featuring their avatars.

Chief Creative Officer Nic Cabana announced the nine-project slate during his closing keynote at Animation Magazine’s World Animation Summit. Heeboo plans to open its first creator communities in January 2027.

“Independent animators and creatives are showing that you don’t have to wait for a studio greenlight to build something people care about,” Cabana said in a release. “With Claynosaurz, we didn’t ask for permission. We started with characters and invited people into the world as we built it.”

The full founding slate includes:

  • El Guapo vs. the Narco Vampires (Jorge R. Gutiérrez) — An original adult animated project from the filmmaker behind The Book of Life, El Tigre, and Maya and the Three.
  • Strawberry Vampire (Emily Brundige) — A YouTube-native animatic series about a family of vampires who feed on strawberries and try to fit into 1950s suburbia. Brundige created Goldie and served as head writer on Hilda and Big Nate.
  • Zooya (Agora Studio) — A world of expressive creatures built around visual comedy. The project already has 169,000 Instagram followers, according to Heebo.
  • Cody++ (Alexander Snow and Joel Foster) — Developed at Double Plus, the project follows a high school freshman who gains the ability to rewrite reality and faces a villain bent on reformatting the universe.
  • Pebbi (Pirogy Studios) — Sofiya Gorokh and Matěj Šak’s digital-clay world of living stones won the Cartoon Forum Direct Access Award at the 2026 CEE Animation Forum.
  • CrittersNom (Joyce Liu) — An original character world from the independent illustrator and motion designer.
  • DeerCat & Friends (Amber Aki Huang) — A character and lifestyle brand that the former DreamWorks designer grew from a personal project into a full-time business.
  • Dead Shift (Kero Entertainment) — A new animated property from the studio founded by two friends from Kharkiv, Ukraine, who built an online following with Patrick Foxy.
  • Claynosaurz (Heeboo Studio) — The company’s flagship character property will be part of the launch alongside the incoming creators.

The slate includes projects that already have a following, such as Zooya and DeerCat & Friends, as well as new work from artists with established careers in studio animation. Heeboo is betting it can give those creators a way to keep fans involved between releases and bring them in while new projects are still taking shape.

Many animators born after the 1965 premiere of A Charlie Brown Christmas cite the holiday special as a formative influence. Directed by Bill Melendez, produced by Lee Mendelson, and written by Peanuts creator Charles M. Schulz, the special remains a holiday favorite more than 60 years later.

Count WildBrain Studios executive producer and writer Mark Evestaff and director Rob “Boots” Boutilier among those animators. They worked on three seasons of The Snoopy Show, among other Peanuts projects. Their first original half-hour holiday special, Snoopy Presents: 12 Days of Snoopy, premiered November 13 on Apple TV.

The last new Peanuts Christmas special was 2003’s I Want a Dog for Christmas, Charlie Brown, directed by Bill Melendez and Larry Leichliter for ABC. In 12 Days of Snoopy, Charlie Brown’s beagle ends the year as a tiny chaos machine, starting unwanted snowball fights and stealing a security blanket. When Snoopy discovers he’s on Santa’s naughty list, Sally and Charlie Brown try to get him back on track in time for Christmas.

Boutilier told Cartoon Brew that making a Peanuts Christmas special was both exciting and a little terrifying. “We had done six segments on The Snoopy Show involving Christmas, and with each one of them, it was a bit trepidatious,” he said. “Like, is this something we should be doing? How do we make sure it’s not stepping n A Charlie Brown Christmas?”

Evestaff said the team drew on years of experience making Peanuts animation to tackle 12 Days of Snoopy. “We were bolstered by years of experience and knowing that we’re working with the same team,” he explained. “There was a lot more confidence going into this that we could pull it off, especially because we weren’t going over territory that had already been explored. This really was from Snoopy’s point of view, but we had the support, the crazy amount of resources and the commitment from our team to be able to make this. There was a lot of hope, but also the opportunity was too big and too good to turn down.”

Boutilier said focusing on a single story “automatically felt different” and gave the team a little more time. “We had smaller animation teams where the animators stepped up to the plate and really took ownership a little more than if we were on a quicker schedule,” he said. “Things like that made the difference. And because the business was going the way it was, or is, it worked out for us because we had access to more talented people that may have been on other projects that were available.”

Evestaff said the special drew artists from across the current Peanuts productions and beyond. “Most artists have some connection to the brand, so it was very easy to get top-tier talent, even if they had other offers on the table, or if they were working on something else; they could moonlight on this. And that’s at every level from the designers to the board artists to the animators. It just has this strong magnetic pull that we were able to keep and then build on the team that we had.”

Boutilier said the Peanuts fans on the crew kept surprising him with details of their own, including an homage to the aluminum trees in the 1965 special.

“When we designed that background, we wanted to make sure that we weren’t copying anything off of A Charlie Brown Christmas,” Boutilier explained. “We wanted to make sure that the tree was stylized, but honestly, I never even thought of it as an aluminum tree until we got the sound back from the sound studio. Their first pass had this aluminum clang, and I was like, ‘Of course it’s aluminum! It should be aluminum!’ There’s always people from different departments thinking back to Peanuts, and they’ll put it in. For me, if it’s subtle, then we keep it in. But we don’t want it to be a blatant callback.”

Making Today’s Peanuts Gang Sound Classic

Voice director Merle Anne Ridley helped the young cast of 12 Days of Snoopy capture the natural delivery of the original specials. “Honestly, it’s a lot of pulling back and [asking], ‘How do you talk to your friends in the schoolyard?’ It really was that simple and pulling back from things they’ve learned.

“One of the reasons we brought in Rerun, for instance, was so [we] had a younger kid, because the kids in the original were younger than kids that we use,” he continued. “It was the idea of [capturing] their innocence, but also the cadence. And if they messed up or couldn’t pronounce a word, we kept it in. That really was a nod to the original, and the authenticity of their delivery, and just being kids. It was a touchstone of what Schulz and Melendez did, and it’s something that we wanted to pay tribute to.”

Boutilier added, “It’s nice when you’ve got a character like Milo, where our voice director is literally sitting next to him in the room, just like they did in the classic specials. She’ll say the line and then he’ll repeat the line, and it’s so endearing. I remember when those recordings came back, both Mark and I were like, ‘Oh, we gotta put more words into this kid’s mouth.’”

New Christmas Songs and a Returning Classic

The special features two original songs, John Legend’s “Get Ready,” produced by Raphael Saadiq, and Kamasi Washington’s “Trying To Get There,” featuring Leon Bridges. Laufey sings “Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas” in a recording produced by Spencer Stewart. Composer Jeff Morrow offers his own take on Vince Guaraldi and Lee Mendelson’s “Christmas Time Is Here.”

Boutilier said the team used the script to identify where songs might fit, then storyboarded those sequences and turned them into rough animatics to share with the songwriters. “If you look at the John Legend sequence with the opening snowball fight, we had the snowball fight boarded and a temp song to keep it in place because we knew somebody would do a song, but we had no idea it would be John Legend,” he recalled. “The sequence itself was fairly tight and formed out, and then they sent the full animatic to John Legend.”

Evestaff said Legend sent back “Get Ready” the same day. “It’s a wild story. It was a month and a half in advance, and they were like, ‘He’s gonna do it this day.’ And we’re like, ‘Really?’ And that day came, and that afternoon we had a song.”

Boutilier and his team dropped the demo into the animatic and adjusted the sequence to fit Legend’s song. “The song that’s in the special is an edited version of the song,” he explained. “The original is quite a bit longer, but it was perfect.”

“Christmas Time Is Here” plays as Snoopy struggles to get back on Santa’s nice list. Boutilier said the idea to include it came from their animatic editor, who’s also a musician. “He put in a version of ‘Christmas Time Is Here,’ not the version from A Charlie Brown Christmas but an interpretation by somebody [else]. It was perfect, but we figured Jeff Morrow was gonna write something else in there anyway. Then the opportunity was there for Jeff to do an interpretation.

“What I love about that moment, and it is one of my favorite moments, is in A Charlie Brown Christmas, that [song] sets the stage and the mood of this is where we’re at. But [here] it’s used so differently, in terms of Snoopy being at his lowest point. It’s sad, but it has joy in it. It’s such an amazing piece of music to be in there. It makes me happy every time I hear that we have this callback to the original.”

Evestaff credited Apple Music with bringing those musicians aboard. “They really are such a massive support with the weight that they throw behind it, and then the knowledge. They also are aware of the legacy, and they wanted to do something special and different, and so they started throwing around these big names, and we’re like, ‘Absolutely! Bring it on.’”

Evestaff and Boutilier singled out a detail for fans of Peanuts creator Charles “Sparky” Schulz. While playing table hockey against Woodstock, Snoopy imagines himself out on the ice.

“Mr. Schulz was a big fan and played hockey throughout his life, and was even a big proponent of older adult tournaments, so it was a big homage to that legacy,” Evestaff revealed. “We put Woodstock in net and I remember growing up playing that little hockey game with my brother. That’s certainly a personal touch, but at the same time the team that animated it, one of the leads is a big hockey player, and you can see it.”

Boutilier said with a laugh, “I can honestly say Mark gave the most notes he’s ever given on the one shot of Snoopy coming around the net and burying the puck. And one thing about that sequence, any Canadian of a certain generation is going to flip out because the music in that sequence is very, very special — it was the theme song of Hockey Night in Canada, which unfortunately doesn’t exist anymore. But it lives on in 12 Days of Snoopy.”

Netflix is taking another run at Matt Wagner’s Grendel, this time as an adult animated series. Bobak Esfarjani (Widow’s Bay, WandaVision, Alien: Earth) will write, showrun, and executive produce, with one of France’s coolest studios, Bobbypills, handling animation.

In a release, Esfarjani said:

Being able to bring a character as iconic as Grendel to life has been a true thrill. Having the support of Matt Wagner, my great EPs, and the awesome team of Netflix, has made it all the more exciting, and partnering with Bobbypills Studio has made it all a true joy.

The announcement comes four years after the streamer scrapped a live-action adaptation of the comic IP. That version, developed by Supernatural showrunner Andrew Dabb, originally got an eight-episode order in 2021 and cast Abubakr Ali as Hunter Rose. Famously, much of the series had already been filmed when Netflix pulled the plug.

An official longline sent by Netflix reads:

After the woman he loves is shockingly murdered, Hunter Rose devotes himself to one thing: vengeance. But as he tears through street gangs, the elite, and New York City’s supernatural underworld in pursuit of her killer, a chance at a real life forces him to choose: walk away from ultimate power, or become the very monster he hunts.

Bobbypills feels a great fit for the project, having previously worked on DC’s Creature Commandos and animated Netflix’s Captain Laserhawk: A Blood Dragon Remix. The French studio’s credits also include the feature Jim Queen and the Quest for Chloroqueer.

Wagner, who executive produced the live-action project, returns in that role alongside Lydia Antonini (Locke & Key) and Dark Horse Entertainment’s Chris Tongue, Tim Wiesch, and Jay Komas.

Of this animated adaptation, Wagner said

It’s incredibly exciting to see my creation finally make this leap to the animated screen! Netflix’s dynamic new series retains the source material’s dark adult themes and also brings a fresh and thrilling approach to the narrative. This is Grendel as I’ve always wanted to see the character portrayed—a hyper-kinetic level of action, bracing explosions of violence and a poignant engaging storyline.

Netflix has yet to announce a voice cast or a release date for this new version, but we’ll keep you posted.

Welcome to Cartoon Brew’s series of spotlights focusing on the animated shorts that have qualified for the 2027 Oscars. The films in this series have qualified through one of multiple routes: by winning an Oscar-qualifying award at a film festival, by exhibiting theatrically, or by winning a Student Academy Award.

Today’s short is The View, an independent film from Pixar vet Alli Sadegiani, inspired by his childhood in Sweden as the son of immigrant parents. It began as a handmade picture book and grew into a short that pairs 2D animation with live-action footage. Sadegiani drew the animation and backgrounds on an iPad using Procreate and Procreate Dreams, and Swedish recording artist Ayla Adams composed her first film score. The short qualified for Oscar consideration through a theatrical run at San Francisco’s Roxie Theater.

Sadegiani wanted the film to feel like reading a child’s diary, right down to the imperfections of handwriting. He took a year off from Pixar to work on it full time, spending more than half of the production on storyboards and the animatic. He shared successive cuts with friends who’d had similar upbringings, using their feedback to decide which of his memories could speak to a wider experience of growing up between cultures.

Cartoon Brew: What was it about this story or concept that connected with you and compelled you to direct the film?

Alli Sadegiani: I grew up in Sweden with immigrant parents during the ’80s and ’90s. It was a very interesting and vibrant period and, in a way, crazy at times. My parents had migrated from a country in chaos following a massive revolution and an ongoing war. They found refuge in Sweden, and while they were forced to start a new life from scratch, I was floating between my parents and this new, foreign world, trying to figure things out.

This was a time when you had classmates who were skinheads, and Nazi salutes on your way to school were part of everyday life. I was still a kid, so I didn’t really have the capacity to question these things. I also formed strong bonds with friends, and the ’80s and ’90s had a lot to offer in terms of pop culture, art, and cinema. Figures like Prince and David Bowie challenged conventional ideas of what it meant to be a man. Growing up amid these contrasting influences helped shape my perspective and laid the foundation for who I am and what I do today.

I never really reflected on these things until much later in life. I identify as a Swede, and I had lived abroad, including in the States, for many years thanks to my work. When the U.S. was grappling with questions of diversity and belonging after 2016, I found myself wondering: Where do I belong?

That sent me down a rabbit hole, digging up a lot of what I had forgotten. Memories of random events from my childhood started to surface and found their way into my sketchbook. I turned those sketches into a picture book, which became the blueprint for what, four years later, would become The View.

It was a very cathartic experience, and I began to share the book with people in my circle. To my surprise, they could identify with many of the same questions and challenges I was touching on, which inspired me to turn the story into a film.

What did you learn through the experience of making this film, either production-wise, filmmaking-wise, creatively, or about the subject matter?

My time at Pixar had taught me a lot about what it takes to get to the core and heart of a film. It’s a brutal process of countless do-overs, and you can’t really take any shortcuts.

Knowing how exhausting this would be, I set up the production to be as lean and efficient as possible. I wanted to be able to change the story or throw things out without having too much impact on the schedule. So I avoided a traditional 3D pipeline entirely and decided to use a very simple 2D setup. Budget was part of the decision, but I also wanted to stay close to the source material, which was the handmade picture book.

I financed the film myself, but I treated it very much like a studio project, showing up to “work” every day with a set deadline and schedule. I even took a year off from Pixar, moved back into my small apartment in Stockholm with my family, and lived off our savings to focus on the film full time. I spent more than half of the total production time working exclusively on storyboards and the animatic, constantly editing and rewriting. I didn’t start production until I felt I had 70–80% of the film there. Once I started, I could put my head down and focus on getting footage out.

That showed me how valuable preproduction and scheduling are. As an indie filmmaker, it’s crucial to get things right before you start, because you won’t have the resources to make changes halfway through.

I made it a habit to share every new version of the animatic with people I trusted. I also kept sending it to friends and people outside the film industry who had the same upbringing as me, to see if it resonated with them. I knew this was going to be a marathon, so on some level I wanted to make sure the film was worth making. Luckily, it turned out there are a lot of people out there still trying to figure stuff out.

Can you describe how you developed your visual approach to the film? Why did you settle on this style and technique?

Since the film grew out of memories from my ’80s and ’90s childhood, I wanted it to feel as if you were reading a child’s diary. I wanted to reference the aesthetic of that time and capture the imperfections of someone’s handwriting, which to me show that we, as humans, are naturally flawed. There’s immense beauty in that. Especially with so much overpolished and artificial imagery around us, I wanted the film’s visual language to reflect what makes handcrafted stories feel human.

An interesting thing about memories is that they’re almost like dreams. They’re captured as images in our heads, and as time passes, we start to question what’s real and what’s an illusion. The live-action footage is an attempt to capture just that: to let the audience experience someone’s memories as blurry and as real as they remember them. I wanted to contrast that footage with designs inspired by Charles M. Schulz, which gave me a gentle, disarming way to approach some heavy topics.

The film draws heavily on your childhood in Sweden. How did you decide which memories to include and which to leave out?

I realized early on that the film was much larger than my own story. While many of the events are unique to me, I felt this was essentially a human journey lived by millions of people every day. So if I was going to take this on, I wanted to make a film that would hopefully help other people find their own way.

Often, I had storylines that touched on the same things in different ways. I had to pick the one I felt served the film best and would resonate with a broader audience.

That isn’t always easy when you’re working on a project so close to you, so it helped to have a circle of trusted friends and colleagues who were brutally honest every time I sent them a new version of the edit.

Floyd Norman accepted an Honorary Oscar over the weekend at the Academy’s 17th Governors Awards in Hollywood. Mahershala Ali presented the statuette to the 91-year-old animator and story artist, who joined Walt Disney Productions in 1956 as the studio’s first Black animator and launched a career that helped define the last 70 years of American animation.

Norman began his acceptance speech well before Disney, with the trips to the movies he took as a kid with his parents. “In that darkened theatrical classroom, I was learning the language of film,” he recalled. He remembered absorbing lessons in lighting, composition, sound, and music. By middle school, he was making cartoons with a 16mm camera his grandmother bought him and a camera stand she helped him build. He made his first feature-length documentary while still in high school.

“I was Alice entering the gates of Wonderland when I visited the Disney studio,” Norman said. He found himself working alongside artists whose films he’d grown up watching. “The veterans were generous, and they shared their considerable knowledge with me,” he said, giving special thanks to “the best mentor a filmmaker could ever have, Walt Disney.”

Norman started as an apprentice in-betweener on Sleeping Beauty, drawing the frames between key poses. After working on One Hundred and One Dalmatians and The Sword in the Stone, he joined the story team on The Jungle Book. The ceremony also revisited his years at Pixar. In a video tribute, Monsters, Inc. director Pete Docter recalled seeing Norman’s storyboards while the team was wrestling with story problems and bringing him aboard to help.

Earlier Sunday, CBS Sunday Morning aired a profile in which correspondent Faith Salie spoke with Norman about his career. The segment recalled how he kept coming into the studio after he was asked to retire, mentoring younger artists.

For 70 years, Floyd Norman brought drawings to life, animating some of Disney’s most beloved stories, like “The Jungle Book” and “Mulan.” And even after he was asked to retire, the first Black animator at Disney kept showing up at the office, mentoring and advising young animators for free.

@Faith_Salie talks with Norman — honored this weekend with a lifetime achievement Oscar — about a career marked by optimism, magic and a wicked sense of humor: “It’s that kind of boundless optimism that keeps me going.”

— CBS Sunday Morning 🌞 (@CBSSunday) November 15, 2026

With all five of his children in the room, Norman recalled packing the family into a Volkswagen van for a vacation in the High Sierras. “Sounds like a bad TV show, doesn’t it?” he said. He thanked his wife, Adrienne, for seeing more work ahead of him when he thought he was done. “In many ways, in many ways, she saved my life.”

Norman closed with a story about a critic who thought the documentary Floyd Norman: An Animated Life could have used more drama. “I could only remind that critic that on occasion, even movies have happy endings,” he said. “And this special evening, here’s my happy ending.”

In Don Bluth: Somewhere Out There, the legendary director behind fan favorites like The Secret of NIMH, An American Tail, and The Land Before Time looks back on his decision to leave Disney and build an independent animation studio. Bluth tells the story himself, recalling what it took to get those films made and why some of his later work fell short of his own expectations.

The feature-length documentary, directed by Dave LaMattina and Chad Walker, follows Bluth from his 1979 departure from Disney through the independent years that produced The Secret of NIMH and An American Tail, and on to his return to studio filmmaking with Anastasia at Fox. Drawing on material from Bluth’s archive at the Savannah College of Art and Design, the film traces the choices he made to keep his studio running, including the compromises he’d once left Disney to escape.

 

LaMattina and Walker, who met at Blue Sky Studios and later made I Am Big Bird, planned to interview a roster of people about Bluth’s career. Their first conversation with the animator put an end to those designs and inspired a redirect towards a more autobiographical endeavor, with Bluth now responsible for reflecting on his career. The good and (a lot of) the bad.

Ahead of the documentary’s November 20 release on Amazon, we spoke with the directors about why they let Bluth tell his own story, what they found in his archive, and what it was like to show him the finished film. We’re also debuting an exclusive clip from the documentary, in which Bluth talks about inspiration and listening to the “blue note.”

 

Cartoon Brew: Why did you want to make a documentary about Don Bluth now?

Dave LaMattina: Chad and I met working at Blue Sky many years ago. I think we’ve always been intrigued by the artist’s process. That started almost by accident when we did this film about Caroll Spinney, who played Big Bird on Sesame Street.

Sometimes the “why now” is answered by the subjects themselves. Don said yes, right? He’s someone who has always held a fascination in our lives. I think there comes a point in every artist’s life when they are prepared to look back and be honest about their journey and themselves. And so the “why now” is partially, yes, Don is still with us. I love, as I think Chad does, to talk to an artist about their art while they’re still living, rather than do a full retrospective with material we have from them.

Sometimes you get someone that’s just ready to talk, and I think Don was very honest in this film. He was very open with us from the beginning, and we took a lot of our cues from him. As he reflected and was pretty honest, that really drove where we were going with the film.

Chad Walker: It was Dave who said, “Hey, this is a really fascinating story about Don Bluth.” And I was like, “Well, someone had to have made this already.” We were both really shocked that no one had. We approached him because we love animation and we love talking to creative people about their process. He was like, “Come on out.”

We went out and talked to him, and I was just blown away by how thoughtful he was, how poetic he was in the language that he would use. All of that influenced the movie, along with the archive we had access to. I think we went into it thinking, “This will just be this kind of straight celebration of Don Bluth because we love all of his movies.” But then you talk to him, and you’re like, “Wow, this is so much deeper than this.” This idea that villains are everywhere and they’re not necessarily people. They can be part of your own personality, like the alter ego. All this stuff fueled his creativity, and we found it really, really fascinating.

Don is very much the narrator of the film. Was that always the plan, or did it come out of those first conversations?

Walker: When we started out, we were thinking, “Okay, this is the basic structure of what this documentary could be.” We had all these people we were going to interview, as we did with the Big Bird movie, to support the narrative. We even had a plan to go to Ireland and talk with some people over there because he had such an influence on that industry.

I know it’s kind of a cliché, but the movie tells you what it’s going to be. From the moment we sat down and started talking to him, we were just so fascinated hearing him talk to us. We were talking about making movies with a legend, and we weave that throughout the movie. He’s kind of teaching us, “Here are all the steps to how to make a good movie.”

Very quickly after that first interview, we dug in and grabbed some of that archival stuff. We were like, “Man, there’s just something really special here about allowing this movie to feel like a conversation between us and a master.”

LaMattina: One of the unsung parts of this film is the archive. Don’s entire archive lives at the Savannah College of Art and Design. SCAD was an awesome partner for us in that they just kind of let us take everything. They had old film reels, they had tapes in every format, and it wasn’t digitized. We were like, “Look, if you let us digitize it, we’ll give everything back to you.”

I think we were the first people seeing a lot of this stuff since it had been captured in the first place. A lot of people aren’t going back and rewatching the outtakes from a canned sales reel that Don is trying to make to sell the movies and stay alive.

I don’t think we were expecting to walk in and find this story that had heavy art-versus-commerce themes. Don is in every single way a pure artist, but his love and his passion are maybe the most commercial of arts there is, and something that you’re really hard-pressed to make by yourself in a garage.

As we started to see what he captured over the years with new eyes, we brought some of our own journey to it. We are not Don Bluth by any stretch of the imagination, but we are people who came from a studio system and decided to leave on our own to do the things that we care about. I think we identified with that journey a lot. Then it was more about, “What is the story that really captures Don for who he is?” His interviews really dictated what the movie became.

Don is candid about what didn’t work. With him telling the story, how did you decide when to challenge his account or bring in other perspectives?

LaMattina: We start on all these things from a place of love, truthfully. We love Don. When we started the Big Bird film, I don’t know that we necessarily would have challenged Caroll to talk about certain things. With Don, I think we’ve done this long enough now that we know it actually is a disservice to a legend like that to not ask some of the hard questions.

This is maybe the first film we’ve done where you do hear our voices in some of the conversation. I can tell you I was very nervous to ask him, “Why did you name the studio Don Bluth Studios when you left with other people?” I was like, “I don’t know how this is going to go.” He answered it in a really honest and awesome way.

He may have answered those questions in the room very honestly and candidly, but when we sat down and watched the film back with him, I was still having full-on flop sweat. I didn’t know how he was going to respond to seeing this come to light on the screen. To Don’s credit, when he watched the film, he was like, “I didn’t necessarily realize that I had this ego that I’m talking about, but I definitely did, and you guys got it.” He was cool with it, which was awesome.

Walker: If we felt in those conversations like he was being false, we probably would have been like, “We need to go find the truth in other voices or other archival talking heads.” But when we sat there, we were like, “Wow, this guy knows.” He knows exactly why those movies didn’t work. He starts cutting corners. The reason why he left Disney, now he’s forced to do the same stuff. To me, that realization on his part was very powerful.

We bring in Siskel and Ebert to tell you, “Yeah, everybody, these movies aren’t working.” Those are the external voices that support what he’s saying. He was just so honest that I personally didn’t think we needed to bring anyone else in to pile on.

LaMattina: Chad edited the film as well, and he has a real brilliance at finding moments in archival footage. I mentioned the canned sales reel before. We have these outtakes where Don is doing the marketing push. I think it was around Thumbelina and A Troll in Central Park.

Chad had the idea to pull from those outtakes to see Don doing the “I’m on camera, I’m trying to sell this because this is something I have to do.” Then you see the moments after they call cut and see Don’s reaction. Don, in those moments, is telling us more than someone looking back and saying, “Oh, well, he had to go commercial.” Paired with the current interviews, I think that’s really telling. It became a much more personal story than I was anticipating at the start of this.

Don had to believe in himself to take on Disney, but he couldn’t have done it alone. How did you make room for the people who built the studio with him?

LaMattina: He is really a true auteur, and we wanted to experience the film through his lens. Don takes the credit, but he also takes the criticism and he takes the failure. If you were to look at who lost to Disney, it would be Don. It’s not anyone else who was at the studio.

I don’t think we thought at the beginning that we were going to be experiencing this as much of an internal war between ego and commerce and faith as we did. It really did feel like we just wanted to live inside Don’s head. All the people who were an important part of it, we showed them through how Don saw it. That was the creative decision, because it is this moment of his life where he’s incredibly introspective. We wanted to live in that memory of his and bring that to life.

Walker: It was important for us that the world knew how important Gary [Goldman] and John [Pomeroy] were. We definitely were like, “Well, they have to be in there.” I feel like we did that through archival footage so that it fit the style of the movie.

There’s one thing he says in the movie that, if you think about it, is like, “Oh, that’s why he couldn’t beat Disney.” It’s when he says he still draws six hours a day. That’s his love. He was never going to stop doing that. That’s the part of everything that he loved. But you could not be as successful as Walt Disney if you’re still drawing six hours a day. He says it very early in the movie, “I wish I was a better businessman.” And that was kind of it. He loved the art.

Bluth’s line about wishing he were a better businessman stuck with me. What surprised you most in those conversations?

LaMattina: He says at some point in the film, “To make a good movie, you need a good script. And we never had one.” And then he says, “We just have to keep people working.” So they have to go ahead.

I saw that firsthand from our time in the industry. We worked with some of the most magnificent artists at Blue Sky Studios. I would put them on par with everyone else out there. It all comes down to story. I’m not critiquing the writers we worked with at Blue Sky. I’m just saying the artistry that Don had was there, and so was that obligation to keep people working and to take care of them.

It’s why Chad and I have purposely stayed very small as a production company and don’t have 300 people or anything. If you wanted to make these big studio pictures, particularly at that time, you needed all these people, and you had to keep them working. You couldn’t go from one project to the next and not have a story, and they just didn’t have the time to do it.

I was really struck by his awareness of that fact. You leave Disney, you do The Secret of NIMH, and it comes out, and it’s all the things that you wanted to do. Then the reality of the business catches up to you and damns you to repeat those same things. Part of it is so admirable because you want to make sure everyone has a job and you want to take care of all these people, but it’s almost tragic to become that thing that you wanted to break free from. Then you have that moment that comes with age of understanding, “Oh, okay, well, I get why they were like that.” That really stuck with me.

Walker: He makes NIMH, which is glorious and everything he wanted it to be. Critics love it, but it’s a commercial failure. You follow that with Dragon’s Lair. They just rush it out. It’s more cartoon than film, and it makes more money than NIMH. It’s a blockbuster. It’s like, “Oh, man, this business is fickle.”

The thing that I connected with the most in the story, and that for me was the most surprising, was Don’s awareness of his ego and how he named them. “The ego is me, but I have this alter ego that fights.” This concept of our ego and how it shapes our behavior is something that really fascinates me. It was very surprising to hear the way he perceived the benefits and the negatives of his ego and alter ego.

At one point in the movie, we’re discussing villains in his life. You see commercial imagery, which could be a potential villain. We see imagery of his father, because he had a rough relationship with him. We go to Roy and Disney because they’re really battling him. And we ask him, “But is an alter ego also villainous?” And he’s like, “Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah.” That, to me, was really shocking, really surprising. I loved our conversations with Don, man. I loved him.

This interview was lightly edited for length and clarity.

Following a hugely unpopular update to Etsy’s terms of use, artists are shutting down their shops in droves and posting illustrated goodbye notes to tell customers where to find them next.

The reason is right there in the online market’s updated terms. Starting December 16, the agreement explicitly gives Etsy and its third-party partners and vendors permission to use content uploaded by sellers to train and improve AI systems.

Ironically, just weeks ago, Etsy announced tighter rules on misleading AI product photos and bot-generated listings. The marketplace still allows sellers to list work generated from their own prompts, as long as they disclose the use of AI to buyers.

Etsy says it uses sellers’ content to spot fraud and help shoppers find products, and that it doesn’t train models designed to copy artists’ work. That said, the vague terms leave open just how its partners and vendors might use that same content.

For an independent animator, an Etsy shop can bring in money between gigs by selling character stickers, prints from a short, or zines of development art. It’s also a popular platform for merch sales that can help finance original projects.

Closing a shop just weeks before the holidays means giving up potential sales, years of reviews, and a storefront customers already know how to find. The artists posting their goodbyes have decided it’s worth walking away from that revenue source to keep their work from being used to train AI.

Etsy will surely continue to run its site and fill the search results with more prints, stickers, and custom pet portraits than anyone could ever scroll through. But when the artists who made the marketplace worth visiting are telling customers where to find them next, why keep sifting through the slop?

Bill Damaschke is stepping down as head of Warner Bros. Pictures Animation (WBPA) as Michael Ouweleen takes charge of a TV animation group that brings Nickelodeon and Cartoon Network under one roof.

Six weeks after closing its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, David Ellison’s Skydance continues to shake up the leadership of some of Hollywood’s biggest and most historic animation studios. On Tuesday, the company told staff that Jennifer Dodge and Traci Balthazor will oversee feature animation at Paramount and Warner Bros. on an interim basis.

Two Labels, One Leadership Team

Damaschke will stay on through a transition period, according to a memo from Skydance Motion Picture Group co-chairs Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein. Like James Gunn at DC Studios before him, Damaschke was brought in to revitalize a corner of the Warner empire and is now moving back into production. The news comes less than two weeks after the release of The Cat in the Hat, the first feature from WBPA under his leadership.

Chris Leahy will continue to run day-to-day operations at the Warner feature studio, reporting to Dodge and Balthazor. John Lasseter and Holly Edwards will continue to lead Skydance Animation.

Who’s The Boss?

Dodge came to Paramount Animation from Spin Master, where she led its entertainment and consumer products business and helped build PAW Patrol into a theatrical franchise. She succeeded Ramsey Naito, who left in October 2025 after more than eight years across Nickelodeon and Paramount. Naito’s teams revived Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, made films based on SpongeBob and PAW Patrol, and developed originals. A year after Naito’s departure, Dodge’s remit now stretches across two feature studios.

Traci Balthazor comes from production, with credits on effects-heavy features including Iron Man, Alita: Battle Angel, and Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes.

Goldberg and Greenstein say the two animation labels will retain separate creative mandates. With Dodge and Balthazor overseeing both, will each studio still be able to greenlight its own films?

Nickelodeon and Cartoon Network Have the Same Boss

Ouweleen’s new Skydance Television Animation group brings together Nickelodeon and Nickelodeon Animation Studios, Adult Swim, Cartoon Network, Warner Bros. Animation, Cartoon Network Studios, and Hanna-Barbera Studios Europe. Comedy Central also falls under his expanded remit.

Peter Girardi and Alec Botnick will report to Ouweleen, with Botnick continuing to oversee Nickelodeon programming alongside Laurel Weir. The reshuffle follows the September departure of Sam Register, who spent 18 years at Warner Bros. Animation and also led Cartoon Network Studios and Hanna-Barbera Studios Europe.

Nickelodeon and Cartoon Network used to compete for shows. Now that both answer to Ouweleen, will they still decide independently which series to commission? Skydance says its animation studios will also sell shows to outside platforms. When the company passes on a project for its own networks, will the studio be able to pitch it elsewhere?

Skydance has told investors it expects at least $6 billion in annual savings within three years. This week’s memos say little about what that means for animation budgets or staffing. Those are the details that will tell us whether the names on the studio doors still represent distinct places to get a film or series made.

On Thursday, November 19, Rockstar Games will release Grand Theft Auto VI, the first new mainline entry in 13 years and, in all likelihood, the biggest entertainment launch ever. On Wednesday, one day before the historic release, the studio’s lawyers appeared in a Glasgow employment tribunal to defend its decision to fire workers who say they were trying to organize.

The case stems from Rockstar’s dismissal of 34 workers in the U.K. and Canada in October of last year. Twenty-three from the group are challenging their dismissals with backing from the Independent Workers’ Union of Great Britain. In their closing arguments on Tuesday, the group’s lawyers described the firings as a “shock and awe” tactic intended to punish union activity. Rockstar denies the allegation and says it fired the workers for gross misconduct after confidential information, including details about game features, was shared on a Discord server.

Rockstar executive Jennifer Kolbe testified in October, denying that she had known about the Discord server for years. Lawyers for the workers argued that Rockstar had been monitoring the server for three years before it took disciplinary action in October 2025. Kolbe said she had met with union representatives in recent months and denied that Rockstar was anti-union. She also said the company had told employees that GTA VI would avoid the kind of crunch that marked earlier Rockstar productions. The tribunal is expected to issue its ruling at a later date.

While the group of dismissed employees awaits the court’s ruling, their former colleagues’ organizing drive is still underway. About 1,600 U.K. Rockstar employees, including staff at Rockstar North in Edinburgh, are eligible to vote on whether the company should formally recognize the Rockstar Game Workers Union. Recognition would give the union a seat at the bargaining table to negotiate with Rockstar on behalf of those workers. The ballot opened November 12 and closes November 26, a week after the game’s release.

Every time Simone pulls a child out of the Seine, the villagers give her a steak. Before long, a suspicious number of children start falling into the French river, and the now-famous Newfoundland is always there to pull them out. In Jon Portman’s animated short Beast of the Seine, locals begin to suspect foul play along the riverbank. Meanwhile, the clever dog has figured out how to get a regular dinner.

The 13-minute short, which premiered online this week, was originally inspired by a 1908 New York Times story about a Newfoundland just outside Paris. As the paper told it, the dog had been knocking children into the water, then jumping in after them to collect the reward. Portman, a San Francisco-based animation director who spent years working in dog training, first came across the clipping on the Instagram account A History of Dogs.

“The dog’s personality practically leaps off the page, and you can tell how much fun the author was having telling the story,” Portman told Cartoon Brew. “It’s rare to find a historical account that already feels so much like a fully formed character-driven comedy. I started writing the next day, partly because I was convinced someone else would stumble across it and beat me to the punch.”

Portman and a small team spent several years making the film, combining digital frame-by-frame animation with hand-painted backgrounds. The village had to feel like it belonged on the outskirts of Paris in 1908, even if the people who lived there looked like they’d wandered in from a contemporary cartoon. Portman brought in painter Charlie Hudson to create many of the backgrounds, with further contributions from Kaitlyn Nguyen and Jui Talukder.

“I’ve always gravitated toward that combination of dark and playful, but finding the right visual language for the film was challenging,” Portman said. “At its heart, this is a comedy, and we wanted the characters to provide a playful contrast to those more traditional, painterly environments. Artists like Matty Kiel, Zack Spakowski, and Max Hodgson helped bring that to life through weird, grotesque, contemporary characters you’d find in something like Ren & Stimpy or Bob’s Burgers.”

The film had its world premiere at the Sedona International Film Festival and went on to win the 12+ audience award at the New York International Children’s Film Festival. It also took both the jury and audience prizes for animated shorts at Durango and Woods Hole.

Notably, Portman’s experience training dogs shaped how he saw Simone. The villagers see a hero every time she brings a child back to shore. From Simone’s point of view, there’s a much simpler lesson in all those steaks.

“We’ve spent thousands of years selectively breeding and training dogs like Simone to perform very specific jobs, and then we’re surprised when they follow those instincts,” Portman said. “I think we make a mistake when we project human motivations onto their behavior, casting them as heroes or villains when they’re really just doing what comes naturally. Ironically, it’s the smelly little kids in the film who seem to understand this intuitively.”
